title: Squashed Hashtag
story: A screen reader reads posts aloud. A hashtag like #lemoncakerecipe is one long run of letters, so the reader tries to cut it into words from a known list and say "lemon cake recipe".
Before it can read the hashtag, it first needs to know whether any clean cut exists.
task: Write canSplit(tag, words). Return true if tag can be cut into pieces that are all in words, and false otherwise.
Every letter belongs to exactly one piece, and pieces keep their order. A word can be used any number of times. The tag has no # and is all lowercase.
constraints: tag and words contain only lowercase letters a to z.

examples.explanation: Cut it as lemon | cake | recipe. The cut lemon | cake | rec | ipe also works, but one clean cut is enough.

The cut start | up | week works. If you grab the shortest matching word first, you take "star" and are left with "tupweek", which cannot be cut into words. So you must be ready to try a different first word.
The cut night | owl leaves a lone "s" at the end. Starting with nigh leaves "towls", and "towel" does not match it. No cut covers every letter.

hints: Suppose you know that the first 7 letters of startupweek, which are startup, can be cut cleanly. What is left to check?
The rest, week, must be one word. In general, the first i letters can be cut if, for some earlier j, the first j letters can be cut and letters j to i form one word.
Keep an array ok where ok[i] says whether the first i letters can be cut. ok[0] is true, since an empty start needs no words. Fill the array from left to right.
For each i, try last-word lengths 1 to 20 (no word is longer). If ok[i - len] is true and tag.slice(i - len, i) is in a set of the words, mark ok[i] true. Return ok[tag.length].
bruteForce: Try every word that matches the start of the tag, recurse on the rest, and backtrack when stuck.

On forty as followed by a b, with words a, aa, aaa, it tries billions of splits of the as before learning the b can never be covered. It asks "can the rest from position 20 be cut?" over and over, and the answer is always the same.

js: * @param {string[]} words  known words, each usable many times
* @return {boolean} true if the tag can be cut entirely into known words
py: def can_split(tag: str, words: list[str]) -> bool:

js: for (const w of words) longest = Math.max(longest, w.length);
// ok[i] = can the first i letters be cut into known words?
for (let len = 1; len <= longest && len <= i && !ok[i]; len++) {
// the last word is tag[i - len .. i)
if (ok[i - len] && known.has(tag.slice(i - len, i))) ok[i] = true;

walkthrough: Every cut has a last word. If it covers letters j to i, the first j letters must be cuttable on their own. So ok[i] is true when some ok[j] is true and tag[j..i) is a word.
Trace startupweek with words star, start, up, week. Positions are letter counts:
• ok[0] is true, because the empty start needs no words.
• ok[4] is true, because "star" is a word and ok[0] is true.
• ok[5] is true, because "start" is a word and ok[0] is true.
• ok[6] is false. The earlier true positions are 0, 4 and 5, and from them the last word would be "startu", "tu" or "u", and none of those is a word.
• ok[7] is true, because "up" follows ok[5]. From ok[4] the last word would be "tup", which is not a word.
• ok[11] is true, because "week" follows ok[7], so the answer is true.
The table keeps every reachable cut point at once, so the dead end after "star" costs nothing, because the cut after "start" is already recorded.
solution.timeWhy: Each of the n positions tries up to L word lengths, and each slice and set lookup costs up to L, where L ≤ 20.
solution.spaceWhy: The program stores the ok table and the set of words.
solution.takeaway: For "can this string be built from pieces" questions, mark which prefix lengths are reachable. Each position looks back by every possible piece length and checks whether the earlier position is reachable and the piece in between is allowed.
